title: Pythagoras’ Theorem

findings.finding: Vary only the longest side to expose the exact equality required for a right angle.
findings.breakdown: The existing parts change several lengths together; none isolates the effect of changing the longest side.
findings.checked: All proposed triples satisfy the triangle inequality. Their squared comparisons are correct, and the converse has been taught in p8-information-block and p8-example-content.
findings.assumptions: Use the existing instruction to decide whether each triangle is right-angled.

repair.proposal: After p9-q2-d, add only this instruction: “Predict each result before calculating.” Add parts e: sides 6, 8, 9; f: sides 6, 8, 10; g: sides 6, 8, 11; h: sides 8, 15, 17. Answers: e not right-angled, since 100≠81; f right-angled, since 100=100; g not right-angled, since 100≠121; h right-angled, since 289=289. In e–g the shorter sides remain fixed while the longest side varies; h is the unpatterned follow-up.

findings.doneWhen: The further parts isolate the longest side before returning to an unrelated triple.

findings.finding: These questions require finding an unknown side in two possible hypotenuse cases before either unknown-side method has been taught.
findings.breakdown: Students must form and solve an equation for an unknown squared length, take its positive square root, and consider whether the unknown or the larger known side is the hypotenuse. Assigning the last entry to the hypotenuse misses required solutions.
findings.checked: Earlier teaching identifies the hypotenuse, writes equations, checks complete triples and generates triads by scaling. p13-q4 supplies a generation formula, but it does not model solving for an unknown side or selecting alternative hypotenuses. Those methods are taught only in later topics.
findings.assumptions: Basic algebra may be prior knowledge, but applying it to both geometric cases is new here. Calculator access does not resolve the missing case selection.

repair.proposal: Before p14-q5, add: “A right-angled triangle has side lengths 5, 8 and x. If x is longest, x²=5²+8²=89, so x=√89≈9.43. If 8 is longest, 5²+x²=8², so x²=64−25=39 and x=√39≈6.24. The side 5 cannot be longest because 8 is larger. Thus there are two possible positive lengths. For a Pythagorean triad, retain only whole-number lengths.”

findings.doneWhen: Before p14-q5, students have seen addition and subtraction cases, the positive square-root step and explicit selection of the possible hypotenuses.

findings.finding: Keep the hypotenuse fixed while increasing one leg to expose how the other leg changes.
findings.breakdown: The existing parts vary both given lengths, so they do not isolate the relationship between the legs for a fixed hypotenuse.
findings.checked: Using the shorter-side method taught in p20-example-content gives the proposed answers 24, 20, 15, 7 and 15. Every triangle is non-degenerate.
findings.assumptions: The new parts continue the existing instruction to calculate side lengths.

repair.proposal: After p21-q1-c, add only: “Predict how the unknown length will change before calculating.” Add right-triangle parts d: hypotenuse 25, known leg 7; e: hypotenuse 25, known leg 15; f: hypotenuse 25, known leg 20; g: hypotenuse 25, known leg 24. Answers: d 24; e 20; f 15; g 7. Follow with unpatterned part h: hypotenuse 17, known leg 8; answer 15. Across d–g only the known leg varies.

findings.doneWhen: Students encounter the fixed-hypotenuse comparison followed by an unpatterned calculation.

findings.finding: The introductory example uses a 13.5 cm leg without explicitly connecting it to the given 27 cm base.
findings.breakdown: Students must recognise that the altitude bisects the isosceles triangle's base. The demonstration labels the half-base but does not state the geometric reason and calculation producing it.
findings.checked: Earlier teaching uses directly labelled lengths or equal-side marks; it does not explain this bisection. The original example marks the equal sloping sides, rather than equal base halves. The equal-half marks in p26-guided-a do not explain the example's substitution.
findings.assumptions: The supplied diagram description shows a half-base label rather than an explicit derivation. Calculator access does not supply the geometric decision.

repair.proposal: Before substituting, write: “The perpendicular height of an isosceles triangle bisects its base, so the right triangle's base is 27 ÷ 2 = 13.5 cm.”

findings.doneWhen: The example explicitly connects the full base to the half-base used in the calculation.

findings.finding: Fix the equal sides and vary the base to expose the relationship between base length and height.
findings.breakdown: The existing parts change the equal sides as well as the base, preventing a direct comparison of this relationship.
findings.checked: All proposed bases are shorter than twice the equal side. Halving each base and applying Pythagoras gives heights 12.0, 10.2, 5.0 and 15.0 cm to one decimal place. The method is available in p26-example-content.
findings.assumptions: The further parts retain the existing instruction and rounding requirement.

repair.proposal: After p28-q3-f, add only: “Predict how the height will change before calculating.” Add isosceles-triangle parts g: equal sides 13 cm, base 10 cm; h: equal sides 13 cm, base 16 cm; i: equal sides 13 cm, base 24 cm. Answers: g 12.0 cm; h 10.2 cm; i 5.0 cm. Follow with unpatterned part j: equal sides 17 cm, base 16 cm; answer 15.0 cm. Across g–i only the base varies.

findings.doneWhen: The fixed-side comparison and unpatterned follow-up appear as further parts of the height question.

findings.finding: The final question requires students to discover a cut and rearrangement before they can use the length methods developed in the exercise.
findings.breakdown: Students must choose an opposite-side midpoint, determine how to move the cut piece and repeat the construction in a second orientation. Earlier demanding questions supply the relevant figures; they do not bridge this dissection search.
findings.checked: The full multistep practice includes local constructions, shared triangles, composite perimeters and repeated applications of Pythagoras. None supplies a rearrangement bridge. Although p38-q13 closes the exercise, the preceding questions do not build towards choosing cuts and moving pieces. The proposed midpoint rotations produce legs 24 and 10, or 48 and 5, giving perimeters 60 m and approximately 101.26 m.
findings.assumptions: No prior dissection strategy is stated. Calculator access does not resolve the construction barrier.

repair.proposal: Add: “Try joining a corner to the midpoint of an opposite side. Rotate the small triangle through 180° about that midpoint. Repeat using the other pair of opposite sides.”

findings.doneWhen: Students can construct both resulting triangles from the cue and independently calculate their perimeters.

findings.finding: Use the same water-surface width above the centre to connect the two possible water depths.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up distinguishes water depth from centre-to-chord distance through the symmetry of the two chord positions.
findings.checked: The half-width is 10 cm and the centre-to-chord distance is √(12.5²−10²)=7.5 cm. The upper depth is 12.5+7.5=20 cm; the original depth is 5 cm, so their sum is the 25 cm diameter. Only methods available by this topic are needed.
findings.assumptions: The pipe remains horizontal and retains the same circular cross-section.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts to p36-q6: (b) “The same pipe is more than half full and its water surface is still 20 cm wide. Find the water depth.” Answer: 20 cm. (c) “What is the sum of the two water depths?” Answer: 25 cm. (d) “Which measurement of the pipe equals this sum?” Answer: its diameter.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up asks one question per part and includes the expected answers.

protectedGroups.observation: The hypotenuse is determined by its position opposite the right angle, regardless of the triangle's orientation.
protectedGroups.varies: Orientation and the positions of the right angle and hypotenuse.
protectedGroups.invariant: A marked right-angled triangle and the instruction to identify its hypotenuse.

protectedGroups.observation: Identification requires established right-angle information rather than appearance alone.
protectedGroups.varies: Presence or absence of a right-angle marker.
protectedGroups.invariant: The request to identify a hypotenuse from a triangle diagram.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the side lengths preserves the right-angle location when the longest side occupies the same position.
protectedGroups.invariant: The right-angled assumption, the longest side at the base, and the reverse-identification task.

protectedGroups.observation: The first three rows give equal squared totals, whereas the final non-right triangle does not; this comparison supports the right-angle condition.
protectedGroups.varies: Side lengths, orientation and finally whether the triangle is right-angled; this is a contrast group rather than controlled single-feature variation.
protectedGroups.invariant: Choose the longest side, square each length and compare a² + b² with c².

protectedGroups.observation: Common scaling preserves the right-angled shape even when the lengths cease to be whole numbers.
protectedGroups.varies: The common scale factor: 2, 1/10, 10 and 1/7, followed by student choices.

protectedGroups.observation: The vertical leg equals the kite’s height only when the string starts at ground level; an elevated starting point requires adding its height.
protectedGroups.varies: The string starts at ground level and then at hand height; numerical measurements also change.
protectedGroups.invariant: The string is the hypotenuse, and the horizontal distance is a perpendicular leg.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing one leg at a time can change whether the exact hypotenuse is an integer or a retained root.
protectedGroups.varies: One known leg length at each transition.
protectedGroups.invariant: The right-angle position, unknown hypotenuse and addition method.

protectedGroups.observation: The same given numbers require different operations when 16 changes from a leg to the hypotenuse.
protectedGroups.varies: The side roles of 16 and x.

protectedGroups.observation: The shorter-side calculation stays the same when the unknown leg changes position and the triangle rotates.
protectedGroups.varies: Placement of the unknown leg and orientation.
protectedGroups.invariant: Hypotenuse 16 cm, known leg 12 cm and the subtraction calculation.

protectedGroups.observation: The roles of the sides, rather than the two given numbers alone, determine addition or subtraction.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether 10 is a hypotenuse or a leg.

protectedGroups.observation: Rotation leaves the hypotenuse calculation unchanged.
protectedGroups.invariant: Perpendicular legs 10 cm and 5 cm, with unknown hypotenuse.

protectedGroups.observation: The same subtraction-and-Pythagoras method applies with the exposed right triangle on either side.
protectedGroups.varies: The position of the sloping side and the numerical dimensions.
protectedGroups.invariant: A supplied perpendicular construction, a base difference giving one leg, and an unknown hypotenuse.

protectedGroups.observation: The outer hypotenuse depends on the sum of the squares of the three successive perpendicular lengths; redistributing those lengths can preserve the result.
protectedGroups.varies: Individual perpendicular lengths and their positions.
protectedGroups.invariant: The joined-triangle structure, unknown outer hypotenuse and exact-answer instruction.

protectedGroups.observation: Moving a given length between the height and a half-base changes which intermediate length must first be calculated.
protectedGroups.varies: The position of the 21 cm given.
protectedGroups.invariant: The 29 cm internal hypotenuse, equal base segments and unknown outer hypotenuse.

protectedGroups.observation: Equality marks determine which length supplies the extra base segment.
protectedGroups.varies: The pair of segments marked equal.
protectedGroups.invariant: The 29 cm internal hypotenuse, 21 cm left base segment and unknown outer hypotenuse.
